title: Second Law of Thermodynamics
short_intro: The second law of thermodynamics establishes the direction of spontaneous thermal processes and dictates that the total entropy of an isolated system can never decrease over time. It sets fundamental limitations on the conversion of heat into work through statements by Kelvin-Planck and Clausius.

exam_scope.tgt_core: Kelvin-Planck and Clausius statements, equivalence of statements, Carnot theorem, Carnot engine efficiency, absolute scale of temperature.
exam_scope.pgt_extension: Clausius inequality, mathematical formulation of entropy change, entropy of ideal gases, principle of increase of entropy, thermodynamic potentials.

prerequisites: Zeroth and First Law of Thermodynamics

concept_notes.heading: Kelvin-Planck Statement
bullets: It is impossible to construct a device operating in a thermodynamic cycle that produces no effect other than the extraction of heat from a single thermal reservoir and the performance of an equivalent amount of work.
This implies that no heat engine can have an efficiency of 100% because some heat must always be rejected to a lower-temperature sink.
It highlights the impossibility of converting thermal energy completely into mechanical work on a continuous basis.

concept_notes.heading: Clausius Statement
bullets: It is impossible to construct a device that operates in a cycle and produces no effect other than the transfer of heat from a cooler body to a warmer body.
Heat cannot spontaneously flow from a colder body to a warmer body without the input of external work, which forms the operational basis for refrigerators and heat pumps.
It establishes the natural unidirectionality of heat conduction.

concept_notes.heading: Equivalence of Kelvin-Planck and Clausius Statements
bullets: The two statements are logically equivalent; the violation of one implies the violation of the other.

If the Kelvin-Planck statement is violated, a cyclic device can convert heat completely into work, which can then be completely converted into heat in a colder reservoir via friction, violating the Clausius statement.

Similarly, if the Clausius statement is violated, heat moves from cold to hot without work input; coupling this with a standard heat engine yields a perpetual motion machine of the second kind, violating the Kelvin-Planck statement.

concept_notes.heading: Entropy and the Second Law
bullets: Entropy is a state function defined via the infinitesimal heat transfer divided by the absolute temperature, dS = dQ_rev / T.
For any irreversible process in an isolated system, the total entropy change is strictly positive (dS > 0), whereas for a reversible process, it is zero (dS = 0).
The principle of increase of entropy dictates that natural processes proceed in the direction of increasing total entropy.

derivations.title: Efficiency of a Carnot Engine
derivations.conditions: Operating reversibly between two thermal reservoirs at temperatures T_1 (source) and T_2 (sink)
steps: Write the net work output of the engine as W = Q_1 - Q_2, where Q_1 is heat absorbed from the source and Q_2 is heat rejected to the sink.
Apply the theorem that the ratio of heat exchanges in a reversible cycle depends only on the temperatures of the reservoirs: Q_1 / Q_2 = T_1 / T_2.
Substitute Q_2 = Q_1 (T_2 / T_1) into the work equation to get W = Q_1 (1 - T_2 / T_1).
Define efficiency η as W / Q_1 to obtain the final expression.

derivations.title: Entropy Change for an Ideal Gas
derivations.conditions: Quasi-static process of an ideal gas
steps: Start from the first law of thermodynamics: dU = dQ - dW, or dQ_rev = dU + P dV.
Substitute dU = C_v dT and P = \frac{nRT}{V} into the heat equation: dQ_rev = C_v dT + \frac{nRT}{V} dV.
Divide both sides by T to get the differential entropy change: dS = \frac{dQ_{rev}}{T} = C_v \frac{dT}{T} + nR \frac{dV}{V}.
Integrate between initial state (T_1, V_1) and final state (T_2, V_2) assuming constant heat capacity.

graphs_and_experiments.title: Carnot Cycle on P-V Diagram
graphs_and_experiments.what_to_draw: A closed cycle consisting of two isotherms (curves) and two adiabats (steeper curves) plotted with Pressure on y-axis and Volume on x-axis.
graphs_and_experiments.interpretation: The area enclosed by the curve represents the net mechanical work done by the Carnot engine in one complete cycle.
graphs_and_experiments.exam_use: Tested in matching processes (isothermal expansion, adiabatic expansion, isothermal compression, adiabatic compression) and identifying work sign.

graphs_and_experiments.title: T-S (Temperature-Entropy) Diagram of Carnot Cycle
graphs_and_experiments.what_to_draw: A rectangle on the T-S plane bounded by temperatures T_1 and T_2, and entropy limits S_A and S_B.
graphs_and_experiments.interpretation: The rectangular area on the T-S diagram directly represents the net heat absorbed (and net work done) by the cycle, Q__net = W = (T_1 - T_2)(S_B - S_A).
graphs_and_experiments.exam_use: Used to compute thermal efficiency visually and compare real cycles with ideal Carnot cycles.

graphs_and_experiments.title: Joule's Paddle Wheel Experiment (Irreversibility Demonstration)
graphs_and_experiments.what_to_draw: Schematic setup of falling weights turning a paddle wheel inside an insulated vessel filled with water, measuring temperature rise.
graphs_and_experiments.interpretation: Demonstrates the complete conversion of mechanical work into heat, but the reverse process (extracting equivalent work from heat to lift the weight without external changes) is impossible.
graphs_and_experiments.exam_use: Conceptual foundation for unidirectional energy degradation and the validity of the second law.

solved_numericals.question: A Carnot engine operates between reservoirs at temperatures of 500 K and 300 K. If it absorbs 1200 J of heat from the source per cycle, calculate the work done by the engine per cycle.
solution_steps: Identify given values: T_1 = 500 K, T_2 = 300 K, Q_1 = 1200 J.
Calculate Carnot efficiency using η = 1 - (T_2 / T_1): η = 1 - (300 / 500) = 1 - 0.6 = 0.4.
Relate efficiency to work and heat absorbed: η = W / Q_1.
Solve for W: W = η \times Q_1 = 0.4 \times 1200 = 480 J.

solved_numericals.question: Calculate the change in entropy when 2 kg of water at 0 °C is heated to 100 °C at constant pressure. Assume the specific heat capacity of water is constant at 4200 J kg^-1 K^-1.
solution_steps: Identify given values: mass m = 2 kg, c = 4200 J kg^-1 K^-1, initial temperature T_1 = 273 K, final temperature T_2 = 373 K.
Use the entropy change formula for condensed phases (constant heat capacity): dS = m c \frac{dT}{T}.
Integrate from T_1 to T_2: \Delta S = m c \ln\left(\frac{T_2}{T_1}\right).

solved_numericals.question: One mole of an ideal monatomic gas expands isothermally from an initial volume of 10 L to 20 L at a temperature of 300 K. Calculate the entropy change of the gas and the universe.
solution_steps: For an isothermal process of an ideal gas, temperature remains constant (T_1 = T_2), so the first term in entropy change vanishes.
Apply the formula \Delta S_{gas} = n R \ln(V_2 / V_1).
Substitute values: n = 1 mol, R = 8.314 J mol^-1 K^-1, V_1 = 10 L, V_2 = 20 L.
Since the isothermal expansion is performed reversibly against a matching external pressure, the entropy change of the surroundings is equal and opposite: \Delta S_{surr} = -5.76 J K^-1.
Calculate total entropy change of the universe: \Delta S_{universe} = \Delta S_{gas} + \Delta S_{surr} = 5.76 - 5.76 = 0 J K^-1 (reversible process).
solved_numericals.answer: \Delta S_{gas} = 5.76 J K^-1, \Delta S_{universe} = 0 J K^-1

assumptions_and_limitations: Reservoirs are assumed to possess infinite heat capacity, meaning their temperatures do not change regardless of heat exchange.
Macroscopic thermodynamic definitions apply to systems in internal thermal equilibrium; entropy is not defined for non-equilibrium states without extension.
Quantum statistical fluctuations can cause microscopic violations of the second law over extremely short time intervals or small spatial scales, but it remains strictly valid for macroscopic systems.

common_misconceptions.wrong: The second law states that energy is destroyed during work conversion.
common_misconceptions.correct: Energy is always conserved (First Law); the second law dictates that energy is degraded in quality and becomes less available for useful work.
common_misconceptions.why: Total energy remains constant, but entropy increases, reducing the fraction of energy convertible to work.

common_misconceptions.wrong: A refrigerator can operate without any external work input if it transfers heat from a cold body to a hot body.
common_misconceptions.correct: External work input is mandatory to pump heat from a lower temperature to a higher temperature.
common_misconceptions.why: Violating this would breach the Clausius statement of the second law.

common_misconceptions.wrong: Entropy of a system can never decrease under any circumstance.
common_misconceptions.correct: The entropy of a specific system can decrease (e.g., when water freezes), but this is always accompanied by a greater increase in the entropy of the surroundings.
common_misconceptions.why: The restriction dS >= 0 applies strictly to the total isolated system (universe), not to open or closed subsystems.

quick_revision: The second law prohibits 100% efficient heat engines and unassisted heat flow from cold to hot bodies.
